title: Block close: always possible
hook: the laws that began with confession end with love
tomorrow: what happens in the gaps a story leaves out?

segments.voice: Yesterday: a plan to return. Name it, repair it, and wait for the same chance. Today the laws of return close, and the last page gets read twice.

The last page of anything gets reread: the final scene of a show, the last text before a friend moved away. These laws of return began with words of confession, out loud: I did this, I regret it, I won't again. And they end in love: a mind sick with love, a love that grows with knowing. One idea runs between the two ends.
screen: `THE LAST PAGE GETS REREAD.` → `IT BEGAN WITH CONFESSION.` → `IT ENDS IN LOVE.`

segments.voice: The idea is this: return is always possible. The door doesn't shut on age or on a long record. In chapter two Maimonides writes that even someone who wronged all their days and returned on the day of their death is forgiven. That's the week's question: how does a tradition hold that door open? And one neighbor holds it open in its own words. Muslims, too, have a word for it that means return, as teshuvah does: tawbah, from a root meaning to turn back. And the Qur'an, in Pickthall's translation, says to people who have wronged themselves: "Despair not of the mercy of Allah, Who forgiveth all sins." That's the shared thread. Two traditions, each with a word that means turning back, each insisting that no one is too far gone to turn. And one honest difference. Maimonides writes as a lawgiver. He lays out the road: the spoken confession, the repair, the test of the same chance, the commandments with their shape. The verse in the Qur'an speaks as a call, addressed straight to the person who has gone too far, telling them not to lose hope. One builds the road; the other calls down it. Neither is a copy of the other, and neither needs to be. Thirty days with this law book, and the last word sounds a lot like the first: always possible.
screen: `EVEN ON THE LAST DAY.` · `TAWBAH: TURNING BACK.` · `DESPAIR NOT OF THE MERCY.` · `ONE BUILDS THE ROAD, ONE CALLS.` · then, large: `ALWAYS POSSIBLE.`

segments.voice: If you can, stand, or shift in your seat, and slowly turn your body to face a different direction from the one you were facing. Let that small physical turn be the whole practice: one turn, made on purpose. Then settle, and breathe in the new direction until the bell.
Block close: thirty days with Maimonides' laws of return, from confession to love. Its last line is always possible.
Last line of the laws: always possible, because no one is too far to turn. Thirty of thirty, the whole block.

howItsDone: Jews return to these laws every year in the month of Elul and the Ten Days of Return before Yom Kippur; Maimonides' Laws of Return is a classic text studied in that season.
